paragraphs.heading: An ice giant
paragraphs.text: Uranus is the seventh planet out from the Sun. It is an ice giant with a cyan colour. Most of it is water, ammonia and methane held in a supercritical phase, material that astronomers call "ice" or "volatiles". Current models place a rocky core inside this icy mantle, with a thick atmosphere of hydrogen and helium wrapped around it. By diameter it ranks third among the planets, and by mass fourth.

paragraphs.heading: Seasons that last decades
paragraphs.text: The axis of Uranus is tipped over by 82.23°, and the planet spins in the retrograde direction, once every 17 hours and 14 minutes. One trip around the Sun takes 84 Earth years. Because of the steep tilt, each pole gets about 42 years of nonstop sunlight and then about 42 years of nonstop darkness.

paragraphs.heading: A cold and puzzling sky
paragraphs.text: The atmosphere is stacked in layers of cloud, and it holds the coldest minimum temperature of any planet in the Solar System, 49 K (−224 °C). Traces of hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide have been found high up, and some of these are thought to have arrived with comets. Much of the weather is still unexplained, from winds peaking at 900 km/h to a shifting polar cap and clouds that form erratically. Uranus also gives off very little inner heat compared with the other giant planets, and the reason is still unclear.

paragraphs.heading: Rings and moons
paragraphs.text: Uranus shares three things with the other giant planets: a ring system, a magnetosphere and many moons. Its rings are extremely dark and send back only about 2% of the light that falls on them. It has 29 known moons: 14 small inner ones, then the five major moons Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon, and far beyond them ten irregular moons. The lopsided magnetosphere is full of charged particles, which may be what darkens the rings and moons.

paragraphs.heading: Mistaken for a star
paragraphs.text: Uranus can be seen without a telescope, but it is dim and creeps slowly against the stars, so ancient watchers never counted it as a planet. Before it was recognised, it was recorded many times and usually taken for a star. The earliest certain sighting came in 1690, when John Flamsteed logged it at least six times and listed it as 34 Tauri. Hipparchus may even have charted it in 128 BC: one star in his catalog does not exist, but Uranus sat at that spot then.

paragraphs.heading: Herschel's comet
paragraphs.text: William Herschel saw it on 13 March 1781 from his garden in Bath, England, using a homemade 6.2-inch reflecting telescope, and at first reported it as a comet. The Astronomer Royal, Nevil Maskelyne, wrote back that he did not know what to call it, since it could be a planet or a comet and showed no coma or tail. Anders Johan Lexell was the first to work out its orbit, and the nearly circular path pointed to a planet. Johann Elert Bode came to the same view, and the object was soon accepted as a new planet.

paragraphs.heading: A bigger Solar System
paragraphs.text: Uranus became the first planet identified with the help of a telescope, and its discovery pushed out the known edge of the Solar System for the first time. Since it lies about twice as far from the Sun as Saturn, the known Solar System roughly doubled in size. About seventy years later, astronomers agreed to name it after Uranus (Ouranos), one of the primordial Greek gods.

paragraphs.heading: One visit so far
paragraphs.text: Only one spacecraft has been there: Voyager 2 flew past in 1986. Telescopes can now resolve the planet, but scientists want to go back. The Planetary Science Decadal Survey made a proposed Uranus Orbiter and Probe a top priority for 2023–2032. The CNSA has also proposed a flyby using a subprobe of its Tianwen-4 mission.
